big_idea: Jim McKelvey argues that durable, defensible companies aren't built on a single innovation but on an innovation stack, an interlocking set of unplanned solutions a company is forced to invent, in sequence, to survive problems with no existing playbook.

tool.label: The innovation stack
tool.text: When an entrepreneur tackles a genuinely new problem rather than copying an existing business, solving it typically creates a new problem needing its own solution, and so on. Each layer depends on the ones below it, so a competitor can't simply copy the top layer, they'd have to independently rebuild the entire stack. McKelvey illustrates this with Square's founding: a lost sale because he couldn't accept Amex led to building a card reader, which ran into 17 different credit-card-network regulations, each requiring its own novel workaround.
tool.note: McKelvey frames the stack as something that emerges organically under survival pressure, not something a company can deliberately plan from the outset.

ideas.title: Perfect problems
ideas.text: The best entrepreneurial opportunities are solvable problems with no existing solution, so there's no playbook or competitor to copy.

ideas.title: Innovation as involuntary
ideas.text: True innovation stacks rarely arise from deliberate choice, they're forced into existence because a founder is blocked at every turn with no incumbent solution to fall back on.

ideas.title: A.P. Giannini and Bank of Italy
ideas.text: McKelvey uses banking pioneer Giannini, who served immigrant and working-class customers ignored by big banks, as a historical example of an innovation stack built long before the term existed.

ideas.title: Timing and enabling technology
ideas.text: Some innovations only become possible once underlying technology matures enough to support them.

ideas.title: Constraints as an advantage
ideas.text: Operating outside an established market means lacking conventional resources, but this absence of how it's normally done can free founders to build genuinely different solutions.

ideas.title: Stacks as competitive moats
ideas.text: Because a full stack is hard to replicate piece by piece, it can protect a company from being out-competed by larger, better-resourced incumbents.

try_it: Write down a problem in your work with no existing solution you can copy, and list every sub-problem solving it would create.
Identify a workaround you use only because no proper tool exists yet, and treat it as the first layer of a potential stack.
Look at a competitor's most defensible advantage and ask whether it's a single feature or an interlocking stack of decisions.
Map the Square and Amex origin story against a frustration you've personally had as a customer, is it a generalizable problem?
best_for: Founders and product leaders building something without an existing playbook
Entrepreneurship-minded readers wanting an alternative to copy-and-iterate startup advice
less_useful: Readers seeking a repeatable, teachable methodology, since McKelvey's own argument is that stacks can't be engineered on demand
Managers inside large, established companies looking for internal-innovation tactics rather than founder-level survival stories

related.why: A more structured, repeatable method for building a new venture under uncertainty
The theory of why incumbents can't easily copy a scrappy new entrant's stack
